title.narrative: Strengthening (teacher) training programmes for tertiary education in agriculture in Uganda

description.narrative:
Impact, outcomes and outputs The project has to contribute to the following impact and must achieve the outcomes and outputs as stated below.
Long-term impact: 1. Reduce malnutrition; 2. Promote agricultural growth; 3. Create ecologically sustainable food systems.
Medium-term impact that will contribute to: (I) Education system (TVET/HE) is of good quality, relevant and accessible (SDG 4); (II) Partnerships between persons and organisations are inclusive and sustainable (SDG 17); (III) Organisations key to (sectoral) inclusive development of partner countries are strengthened by inflow of enhanced workforce.
Outcomes of the project: A. TVET/HE organisations (in the selected partner countries and in NL) perform better their core tasks, firmly embedded in their environment (in line with country / regional specific labour market needs & aiming at inclusiveness); B. Enhanced knowledge and skills of individuals and organisations in line with country / regional specific labour market needs & aiming at inclusiveness (in partner countries and in the NL).
To that end, the following output(s) must be achieved by the end of the project: 1. Established network of TVET/HE institutions, private sector, MoE and selected NGO’s about the development of a learning line and interlinked teacher-training programme in agro-enterprise on certificate, diploma and degree level. 2. Developed policy framework (including national core competences and accreditation mechanisms) for agro-enterprise education for informal, TVET and HE education. 3. Pilot by NICA, its feeder schools, KyU and HUAS on the development of a learning line and interlinked teacher-training programme in agro-enterprise, in collaboration with the private sector and regulatory bodies in the prioritised agricultural domains. 4. Expertise developed at NICA, its feeder schools and KyU for the implementation of a learning line and interlinked teacher-training programme in agriculture, aiming at inclusiveness. 5. Development plan for integrated TVET/HE learning lines and interlinked teacher-training programmes in Uganda.

description.narrative: Reporting is an important management tool which is used to inform relevant government officials and other stakeholders about the results being achieved by individual projects and the programme as a whole. For project partners, it is compulsory to use the prescribed Orange Knowledge annual report format in order to report on project achievements. The annual report also provides valuable data on the financial situation of the project. Based on an analysis of the project performance in relation to the project output(s) and expected outcome(s), a revision of the project work plan may be suggested by the project partners. The consequences of a possible revision on the project work plan and budget must be made clear in the annual report. Nuffic monitors outputs and outcomes and not activities . Therefore, the main focus of the annual report must be on the achievement of the project’s output(s) and planned outcome(s). The information provided in the annual reports of the projects is used by Nuffic to monitor the progress of the project and to inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other stakeholders about the output(s) and outcome(s) being achieved by individual projects and the Orange Knowledge programme as a whole. Please note that if project progress is in accordance with the original planning, reporting requirements are minimal. Only in case of deviations from the planning, more elaboration is demanded. In the grant award letter, the dates for submission of the annual reports are mentioned. In case of a three-year project, between 5-7 reports are obligatory. The first report (0) is a very short report which focuses on specific conditions and/or recommendations in the grant. There is no need to report on progress in achieving outputs and outcomes, which is done in the first annual report. title.narrative: 7. Holistic approach towards capacity development

description.narrative: What progress is being made in strengthening the overall capacity of the requesting organisation to deliver the products and services which are demanded by the labour market and society in general. Please differentiate between institutional, organisational, individual and educational capacity needs. please highlight the progress in procurement of investments and explain how the hardware is integrated in teaching/education. What successes and or constraints can be reported in relation to integrated capacity development and the 5 Capabilities ?

actual.value:
**Organizational** In this OKP project NICA is working closely together with a large number of stakeholders: training institutions, farms/companies, governmental partners and NGO’s. This is very important for the visibility of the college. Very often funds of e.g. the government and NGO’s are invested in educational institutes around Kampala as representatives simply don’t take the time to travel up North and visit colleges situated over there. Through this project, the Minster of Education became very interested in the college, which open the doors for new investments and additional staff.
**Institutional** NICA is currently blessed with a strong management team, consisting of a principal, vice-principal, deans and heads of departments. The team works efficient and in good harmony, staff members are involved in decisions making. The project management have requested the Governing Council (GC) and the Ministry of Education (MoE) to leave the team in the same composition until the end of the project, even though some staff members are reaching the retirement age before the end of 2021. An oral confirmation is already received, the college is still waiting for a written confirmation. Discussions with the GC and MoE will be continued during the project period, making sure that there will be a good replacement plan.
**Individual** The location of the college is not very attractive for staff members as it is located in the North . The nearest city (Lira) is a 45-minute drive by car and there is a shortage of staff housing at campus. Therefore, motivation of staff members is very important. The OKP project supports the motivation by providing an irrigation system, so fresh food can be harvested year around and staff can also eat healthy food during the dry season. Besides this, staff members will get the chance to upgrade their skills and knowledge while attending training sessions.
**Educational** The new curriculum is drafted in close cooperation with companies/farms and they have signed Cooperation Agreements stating their continues support to NICA. The buy in from companies/farms will make the program more attractive for current and future students.
**Investments** The first investment in the project is the development of an irrigation system for the school farm. For this purpose, the college had to drill a borehole on the land of the college neighbour, as this was the most promising place to find a large quantity of water. The neighbour wanted to provide the land for free, but the Governing Council have developed an official agreement, in order to prevent problems in the future. For other small investments (like the development of a piggery), the college followed the rules and regulations of the Ugandan government for investments.
**Successes and constrains** The implementation of the project is above expectations. A number of outcomes planned for year 2 are already achieved in the 1st year. Staff members of NICA and KyU are very motivated for the development of the new curricula as the old curricula are very outdated.
The biggest constrains for the implementation of the project are: - Change in the educational system (upgrade from diploma to bachelors level) - Staff qualifications (current staff is not allowed to teach on bachelor level) - Staff retention (location is not popular) - Change of management (many are about the retire)

**Organizational**
Through this OKP project, NICA strengthened its relationship MoE and KyU and got the opportunity to present itself. Representatives of both organization have paid several visits to NICA and became aware that the college plays a very important role in the development of skills education in the country. Very often funds are invested in educational institutes around Kampala as representatives simply don’t take the time to travel up North and visit colleges situated over there.
**Institutional**
NICA experiences difficulties with retaining staff members as several important individuals have reached the retirement age (Principal, HoD Agriculture) and others are went for further studies or found a position outside the remote areas of the country. When the college opened its doors after the Covid lock down, many staff members started at a new position, but still some empty seats are not filled by the government. However, the existing team in strong and determined to provide the students with high quality, skills based education.
**Individual**
The location of the college is not very attractive for staff members as it is located in the North. The nearest city (Lira) is a 45-minute drive by car and there is a shortage of staff housing at campus. Therefore, motivation of staff members is very important. The OKP project supports the motivation by providing fresh food from the school farm year around. Besides this, staff members get the chance to upgrade their skills and knowledge while attending training sessions.
**Educational**
The new curricula have been drafted in close cooperation with companies/farms and NICA have signed MoU’s with these stakeholders stating their continued support. The buy in from companies/farms will make the program more attractive for current and future students. Besides this, the new curricula are skills based, which gives graduates more chances to find a job after they have finalized their studies. This could be in the educational sector, but also in the private sector e.g. as team leader in a private farm.
**Investments**
The project have invested highly in the school farm as it serves multiple purposes. In the first place, it gives agri students the chance to practice their agricultural skills, in the second place, it gives them the opportunity to practice their entrepreneurial skills and finally it feeds the whole NICA community (students and staff members). The college followed the rules and regulations of the Ugandan government while purchasing:
- Irrigation system - Fencing materials - Pick-up truck - Building materials for the piggery
**Successes and constrains**
The development of the school farm is one of the big successes of the project, it is visible for students and staff members and makes the campus a more attractive place to live and study. Another success is the development of additional study programs in electrical, mechanical and automotive engineering. The NICA study programs are closely related (sharing the same didactical modules) and therefore redeveloping one out of seven programs gives difficulties in the implementation phase.The biggest constrains for the implementation of the project are:
- Delay in project implementation because of Covid measurements - Staff retention (location is not popular) - Change in the educational system (upgrade from diploma to bachelors level)

title.narrative: 6. Labour market and entrepreneurship

description.narrative: What progress is being made to relate higher education and TVET to the demands of the labour market? What are the prospects of graduates to find employment or to become self-employed?

actual.value:
Curriculum activities for all study programs (Agri, Electr. Mech. and Autom.) started with visits to companies in the respective areas. On top of that NICA organized a local network meeting and signed MoU’s with important stakeholders in the agri sector.
Even though NICA is educating technical instructors for the Ugandan training institutions, some students have the desire to start their own farm. The new curriculum and the school farm experiences provides them with the necessary skills, attitude and confidence to become successful entrepreneurs.

One of the first activities of the project was a national network meeting bringing a large group of educational institutes and companies in the agricultural sector together. These representatives of companies gave input for the new curricula during a 2-day workshop. On top of this staff members of NICA and KyU staff visited a number of companies around Lira, followed by a regional network meeting at the campus of NICA.
Even though NICA is educating technical instructors for the Ugandan training institutions, some students have the desire to start their own farm. The new curriculum and the school farm provides them with the necessary skills, attitude and confidence to become successful entrepreneurs.
